tool.intro: When an anxious thought takes over, this worksheet guides you step by step to examine it, as is done in cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). The aim is not to 'think positive', but to find a fairer, more balanced view.
tool.privacy: Nothing is saved: your answers are erased when you leave the page. You can download the worksheet as a PDF to keep it or show it to your clinician.

s1.title: The situation
s1.help: What happened? Where, when, with whom? Describe the facts, as a camera would have filmed them.
s1.placeholder: For example: my manager asked me to come and see him at the end of the day.

s2.title: My emotions
s2.help: What did you feel? Choose one or more emotions, then rate their intensity.

s3.title: The thought
s3.help: What went through your mind at that moment? Write the thought down as it came.
s3.placeholder: For example: 'I'm going to get fired.'
s3.belief: How much I believe this thought

s4.title: Thinking traps
s4.help: When anxious, the mind often falls into the same traps. Do you recognise one in your thought?

traps.name: Catastrophising
traps.desc: Imagining the worst and seeing it as certain.

traps.name: Fortune telling
traps.desc: Being sure things will go wrong.

traps.name: Mind reading
traps.desc: Believing you know what others think of you.

traps.name: All or nothing
traps.desc: Seeing things in black and white, without nuance.

traps.name: Overgeneralising
traps.desc: Drawing a rule from a single event ('always', 'never').

traps.name: Negative filter
traps.desc: Only noticing what goes wrong and forgetting the rest.

traps.name: Emotional reasoning
traps.desc: 'I feel it, so it must be true.'

traps.name: 'Shoulds' and 'musts'
traps.desc: Rigid demands on yourself or others.

s5.title: The facts
s5.help: Like a detective, look for concrete evidence — not impressions.
s5.placeholderAgainst: For example: my last review went well; he often calls people in about practical matters.

s6.title: Another view
s6.help: These questions can help you find a more balanced thought:
questions: What would I say to a friend who had this thought?
What is the worst that could happen? The best? The most likely?
If the worst happened, how could I cope?
How will I see this situation in a month, in a year?
s6.placeholder: For example: 'I don't know why he wants to see me. It may be something practical, and even if it's criticism, I can discuss it.'
s6.belief: How much I believe this new thought

s7.title: Summary
s7.help: Reread your new thought. How do you feel now?
s7.noChange: If the emotion hasn't dropped much, that's not a failure: questioning thoughts is a skill, and the effect grows with practice.

howItWorks.title: How This Worksheet Works
howItWorks.description1: It isn't only situations that cause our emotions, but also how we interpret them. When anxious, these interpretations are often more threatening than reality, and they come so fast that we don't notice them.
howItWorks.description2: The worksheet helps you slow down: describe the situation, spot the emotion and the thought, examine the facts, then look for a more balanced view. You don't replace a negative thought with a positive one: you look for a fairer one.
howItWorks.description3: It is a core tool of cognitive behavioural therapy. It is often easier at first to fill it in with a clinician, then to use it on your own.

notice.title: Spot
notice.description: Notice the thought that comes with the emotion.

examine.title: Examine
examine.description: Test the thought against the facts, like a detective.

rebalance.title: Balance
rebalance.description: Find a fairer thought, neither dark nor rosy.

science.title: What Studies Say
science.description: Examining your thoughts is one of the tools of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), the most studied psychological treatment for anxiety. The worksheet alone has not been evaluated: studies look at the full therapy, with a therapist.
science.bottomLine: CBT genuinely helps many anxious people. This worksheet uses one of its tools: it can help you step back, and works better as part of professional support.

carpenter.title: CBT compared with placebo
carpenter.who: About 2,800 patients with an anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder or post-traumatic stress.
carpenter.what: CBT compared with a placebo (an inactive pill or simple supportive counselling).
carpenter.result: CBT was more effective than placebo (medium effect), especially for generalized anxiety and OCD, and benefits were maintained over time.
carpenter.caution: Less clear effects for panic disorder, social anxiety and post-traumatic stress; possible publication bias.

recent.title: The most recent trials
recent.who: About 1,250 adults, in trials published since 2017, mostly on post-traumatic stress.
recent.result: CBT remained more effective than placebo, but with a smaller effect than in older syntheses.
recent.caution: Few recent trials on other anxiety disorders; results rely mainly on post-traumatic stress.

whenToPractice.title: When to Use It
items: When an anxious thought keeps coming back and weighs on you
After a situation that worried you a lot, to review it calmly
To prepare for an appointment with your psychologist or psychiatrist
Regularly, to learn to spot your usual thoughts

whatYoullNotice.title: What You Might Notice
items: That emotions are often linked to an interpretation more than to the facts
Thinking traps that keep coming back for you
An emotion that eases a little once the thought is balanced
With practice, being able to do this faster, in your head

calm.title: When calmer
calm.description: In the middle of a crisis, start by breathing or grounding; the worksheet works better once you've settled a little.

honest.title: Fair, not positive
honest.description: A balanced thought should feel believable. If it rings false, keep looking.

together.title: With a clinician
together.description: Bring your worksheets to your psychologist or psychiatrist: they are an excellent starting point.
